**Talk about Knowing**
**A. C. LLOYD**
In this article I wish to suggest a new approach to an old question, the
question whether knowing something entails the impossibility of being
mistaken about its truth. It will lead to a negative answer to the question,
but by a line of argument which will also contain a possible (and I think
neglected) explanation why an affirmative answer is so tempting. I shall
assume that knowledge is based on evidence, or (to speak more neutrally)
restrict myself to such knowledge. The nature and cogency of the
evidence is only indirectly my concern; so the term 'conclusive' will be
used to indicate neither more nor less than the fact that someone's
evidence for _p_ is sufficient evidence for him to know _p._ What is being
asked is whether, if someone has such evidence (and, let us say, infers _p)_
he can _falsely_ believe the truth of _p._ This ia not always the same as asking whether _p_ can, still less asking whether it could, be false, for that
might be asking merely whether it was contingent. But of course 'it may
be false that p' commonly is equivalent to 'you may be wrong', namely
when neither the first is meant as the trivial consequence of ' "p" is contingent' nor the second as that of ' "you are right" is contingent'.
Certainly it is a necessary truth that if 'p' is known 'p' is true; and no
doubt some people have confused this with a claim that if 'p' is known
'p' is a necessary truth. <sup>1</sup> But I hope to shew that there is more behind
the demand for conclusiveness to exclude the possibility of error, and
hence for a distinction between knowing and any kind of believing, than
that confusion. The reason is that the rules for 'must be' and 'may be'
in ordinary discourse do not coincide with those for the necessity and
possibility of ordinary modal logic. <sup>1</sup> That on the contrary they sometimes
represent 'epistemic' modalities has of course been claimed by various
philosophers (for instance, Frege), and everyone is indebted to Jaakko
Hintikka for a systematisation of them.* In this article the purpose is
different. It is to shew how the usage of ordinary discourse does differ
from that of modal logic _without_ having to represent epistemic modalities.
It is that difference, independent of any particular concepts of knowledge,
which bears on our question of the relation of conclusive evidence to
infallibility.
So as to make the material clear it is presented not as reports of what
can be thought about some situation involving or thought to involve
knowledge and evidence but as exphcit expressions of such thoughts by
participants in the situation. To give the simplest of examples, we are
going to be presented with conversations in which somebody says that
1 A good deal of weight is still put on this confusion: see e.g. the opening
of J. Harrison's carefully argued paper, 'If I know, I cannot be wrong',
_Proc. AT. SOC.,_ lxxviii (1979), pp. 137-150.
_2_ Cf C. L. Karttunen Tossible and must", in J. P. Kimball (ed.) _Syntax and_
_Semantics,_ vol. 1 (N.Y.: London, 1972).
3 See particularly _Knowledge and Belief_ (Ithaca, N.Y., 1962).
263
264 A. c. LLOYD:
something is known and somebody else asks how. It would have been
possible to have dispensed with direct speech and talked about the
situations, even in the case of the more sophisticated interchanges.
I mention this only in case the reader might otherwise have been suspicious
of the method. It is not that kind of appeal to ordinary language against
which someone can object that he would not have said what is being
said to be said. All that matters is that the conversations should be
possible ones. The task is then to understand them in a way which
makes sense of them—makes a coherent interpretation of them, and so
reveals genuine or non-contradictory concepts. Whether other conversations would reveal alternative concepts is another question. There
are more pressing reasons for preferring direct speech. There are distinctions which depend on tense and person, so that reported speech
would anyway have been called for; and one crucial point will depend,
as we shall see, on the fact that a sentence is asserted.
II
Jones has pestered Miss Patagonia 1978 on a voyage. But she is a fairminded woman who knows that some licence is perhaps to be allowed to
passengers on a ship. Her uncle, the Patagonian ambassador, is not only
fair-minded but a reflecting not to say pedantic man; he believes that
for Jones's misbehaviour to be mitigated Jones must not merely have
been on a ship at the time but have known that he was on a ship. It is
that knowledge which will be in question. A. is the first interchange.
Miss Patagonia: Jones knew that he was on a ship.
Ambassador: How did he know?
Miss P: He could see waves, he had a steamship ticket to
Liverpool, people were behaving like people on
a ship, etc. (E 1)
Ambassador: Even so he might have been on shore.
Miss P: Yes, but he wasn't.
Ambassador: How do you know?
Miss P: I was there..., I am now in Liverpool, and I
certainly didn't come from Valparaiso in an aeroplane, etc. (E a)
Some preliminary points first. The form in which the evidence for
Jones's knowledge and the evidence for Miss Patagonia's knowledge—
abbreviated as Ei and Ez respectively—are stated is fairly casual. It is
not intended to provoke questions about direct experience and the like.
Nothing hangs here on what exactly counts as evidence. On the other
hand it must be borne In mind that whoever knows that p _has_ evidence
that p; it may be the case but is irrelevant that there _is_ evidence for every
true proposition. The 'etc' while certainly not intended to indicate some
quasi-infinite series which would entail the proposition said to be known,
is intended to indicate a true description of the evidence possessed by
the person in question and, roughly speaking, a complete one.
TALK ABODT KNOWING 265
The problem we are concerned with at present is the force of 'might
have been' in the ambassador's second speech. It would not be natural
here, even for a pedant, for it to mean 'even if Jones was on a ship it
could have been the case that he was not on a ship because the contrary
of every matter of fact is possible.' This would draw attention merely to
the fact that 'x is on a ship' represents a type of contingent sentence. The
natural interpretation of it is as a concealed argument against the assertion
that Jones knew he was on a ship. 'Even so' refers to Ei, and the
ambassador is saying that 'Jones was on a ship' could be false and Ei
true. What he is saying implies that Ei does not entail 'Jones knew that
he was on a ship'; and Miss Patagonia puts a natural interpretation on
it when she takes the implication to rest on the impropriety of Jones
being aaid to know something which may not have been the case. She
could, it may be suggested, have taken the impropriety to consist in his
being said to know something on inconclusive evidence. This (as will
become clearer) is a different interpretation because 'evidence' in it
would refer to evidence possessed by Jones. But she did not need to
understand the Ambassador in this way. And she does not. Otherwise
she would have said something lilw 'No he couldn't' or even 'If that's
what you think nobody can know anything'. It follows that the 'might
have been* (or synonymously 'could have been') is not grammatically
counterfactual but merely the past tense of 'may have been'. The
ambassador could just as well have said 'For all that (viz. Ei) Jones _may_
have been on shore' or 'For all that it may be the case that Jones was
on shore <sup>1</sup>. We have only to imagine him saying to himself *With the
amount they drink it's just as likely they were in a fairground*. There
are reasons why the past tense, though equivalent, should be preferred:
but they are more linguistic than logical. His argument then is to the
effect, 'For all the evidence you have it may be the case that Jones was
not on a ship, so you can't say that he knew he was'. _It is not Jones who_
_is at fault (by not having been able to know), according to the argument, but_
_Miss Patagonia for saying he did._ So far as _she_ accepts the 'might have
been' it is of course counterfactual. For she produces additional and
independent evidence that he was on a ship. Not only does this not mean
but it cannot mean that she is trying to remedy the inconclusiveness of
Ei on the assumption that Jones could not have known something unless
he had evidence which was conclusive. If that had been the intention the
additional evidence, E2, would not have helped, for it is evidence possessed
now by Miss Patagonia, not then by Jones. Notice incidentally that being
in the context of, even dependent on, evidence does not make a _'may be'_
epistemic: it belongs just as much to ordinary logic as the 'some S may
be not-P' that is used to contradict somebody who claims that all S is P
on the grounds that all M is P and all M is S.
But why should the fact that Jones may not have been on a ship prevent
a person from saying (truly) that Jones knew he was on a ship? The
explanation is that it is not that fact which would prevent the person
but only his acknowledgement of it. _A conjunction of the form' p but it_
_may be that not p' cannot properly be asserted._ This will include the
assertion 'x knew that p but it may be that not p' since 'x knew that p'

implies 'p\ Suppose I am asked for the telephone number of the
Patagonian embassy. I might say 'It may be in the directory*. If I then
look into the directory I can say 'It is in the directory* or I can say 'It is
not in the directory* or I can repeat 'It may be in the directory*; I can
also say 'It is not in the directory but it might have been' or 'It is in the
directory but it might not have been*. Each utterance would be readily
understood. What I cannot say, and mean what I say, is 'It is in the
directory but it may not be' or 'It is not in the directory but it may be*.
There are only two obvious ways of making sense of the form 'p. it may
be that ~p*—a form, it should be noticed, which is independent of the
tense of 'p*. Either (a) what is meant is 'p, but on second thoughts it
may be that ~ p ' or (b) what is meant is 'I think that/probably p, but
it may be that ~p*. Either way the form 'p. it may be that ~p* will have
been surrendered: with (a) we no longer have a logical conjunction which
is asserted (i.e. simultaneous assertion), with (b) 'I think that/probably p'
is not the same assertion as 'p*.
The linguistic rule, 'a conjunction of the form "p but it may be that
^ p " cannot properly be asserted' has a feature to which I now wish to
draw attention. It is a rule about asserting, not about the sentences or
sentence forms as such. The meanings of sentences of the forms 'p' and
'it may be that ~ p ' are not such that 'p->-~(it may be that ~p)' is
analytic. For what _general_ meaning, in terms of inter-sentential implication, can we find for 'it may be' except what is familiar in modal logic
either as possibility (Lewis's~D~) or contingency (<—'D~. ~D)? But
with neither interpretation can we have 'p. it may be that ~ p ' as a logical
contradiction. To try to do so would be self-defeating since it would be
at the price of having 'p', 'it may be that p' and 'it must be that p' all
logically equivalent. The upshot is that 'p. it may be that ~ p ' is a socalled paradox of a pragmatic or 'Moorean' kind like 'p. I don't believe
that p', not a contradiction. In Hintikka's system (i) 'it may be that p' is
interpreted as 'I do not know whether p' and this as 'I do not know that
p and I do not know that ~ p ' and (2) sentences whose truth logically
couldnotbeknownbythe speaker are absurd ('epistemically indefensible').
'p. and it may be that ~ p ' would then obviously be such a sentence. My
position here is incompatible with (1): but I see no compelling reason
for accepting either (1) or (2).
Now let us suppose a flashback to the scene which took place a few
days earlier.
B
Jones: I know I am on a ship.
Miss P: How do you know?
Jones: I can see waves, I have a steamship ticket to Liverpool,
people are behaving like people on a ship, etc. (E 1)
Miss P: You could still be on shore.
Jones: I could _have_ been, but I'm not.
Miss P: How do you know?
Jones: As I have already told you, E 1.
TALK ABOUT KNOWING 267
Here 'could still be on shore' again means '"Ei" may be true and
"you are on a ship" false. (If Miss Patagonia is herself confident that
they are on board she is being captious or else sly, insinuating perhaps
'in the condition you are in'). But 'could have been' must in this case be
a rhetorical allusion to the contingency of the fact that he is on a ship—
and not necessarily one which is trivially true: one could imagine an
unspoken thought of Jones's, 'If you recall, I suggested that we should
forget the sailing and go to my apartment'. For B differs from A in the
fact that Jones cannot afford to admit that Ei does not imply that he
cannot be mistaken about being aboard, for the admission would imply
that his evidence was inconclusive. (It would not be the trivial admission
that the proposition is contingent.) Suppose Jones had replied 'Yes,
I could still be, but I'm not', Miss Patagonia (if she had had her uncle's
logic) would have pounced on this and retorted, 'Then it is only probably
true that you are not ashore, and for you to add "but I'm not" is childish
because we are interested in what you know not what you are prepared
to assert.' In A the admission could be made because further evidence
(E2) could be produced for the truth of what was claimed to be known.
This rests on an epistemic difference: Ei was claimed as Jones's
evidence, E2 was Miss Patagonia's. In B Jones, unlike Miss Patagonia,
has already used his evidence (which we agreed should be all the evidence
he had). When he says he might have been on shore he cannot mean to
agree that for all the evidence he has he may not be on a ship. For that
would either have to be interpreted to imply that he had changed his
mind about knowing and meant something like 'I haven't got proper
grounds but that's what I believe'. This possibility does not interest us
because the concept of knowledge would no longer be in question.
Alternatively it would have to be interpreted to mean that he was
prepared to say 'I am on a ship but I may not be on a ship*. The consequence is that he cannot admit, that is to say assert or be prepared to
assert, that the conclusiveness of his evidence is compatible with his
being mistaken.
There is therefore a linguistic difference between B and A. What
different features in B have brought it about? The claim to knowledge
in B is in the first person whereas in A it is in the third person. But it
must not be concluded that this accounts for the different treatment of
evidence. The following interchange concerns first person knowledge
but it is on all fours with A, not B.
Jones: I knew that I was on a ship.
Ambassador: How did you know?
Jones: I could see waves, I had a steamship ticket..., etc.
Ambassador: Even so, you might have been on shore.
Jones: Yes, but I wasn't.
Ambassador: How do you know?
Jones: Well, I was in Valparaiso last week, and I'm in
Liverpool now, and I certainly didn't come in an
aeroplane.
**268** **A. C. LLOYD: TALK ABOUT KNOWING**
This was to be expected. From an epistemic point of view Jones is
now a different person from what he was, for _his_ evidence now does not
have to be _his_ evidence then.
For the same reason we can get the critical distinction between Ei and
Ez when we have a present tense claim to knowledge, provided that it
is not in the first person.
D
Miss Patagonia: Jones knows that he is on a ship.
Ship's chaplain: How does he know?
Jones: You know that you are on a ship.
Miss Patagnonia: How do you know?
D and E can obviously continue like A.
In short, there are four grammatical combinations of tenses and persons
possible in assertions of knowledge: present or past, first person or other
than first person. Of these _only assertions in the present tense and first_
_person exclude the admission by the assertor that even on the assertor's_
_evidence what is asserted to be known may not be/have been the case._
What has led to this has various implications for the concept of
knowledge. Among them these can be noticed now. Evidence for what
ia known does not have to exclude the possibility of error. For in the
first place take the present tense first person cases represented by B,
and assume that the hypothesis of possible error does not follow merely
from the fact that the proposition known is contingently true. Even there
the admission of the possibility does not have to be construed as a
contradiction. The reader must decide how much weight to put on this
point. But secondly, when the knowledge is reported of someone else
the admission is not even a paradox of assertion. There is a further
implication that there is a potent reason for the mistaken belief that
evidence which is sufficient for knowledge is sufficient to guarantee truth
by excluding the possibility of error. This is the special but misleading
present tense first person cases, which for understandable but dubious
reasons have commonly been considered the standard cases. This potent
reason is independent of any confusion between 'D[(it is known that
p)->-p]' and '(it is known that p)->-Dp <sup>></sup>, <sup>1</sup> and indeed of anything special
about turning at all.
**UNIVERSITY OF LIVERPOOL**
